title: NJ refusal, capacity, consent and DNR/POLST
body:
Sources, all current as written:

- **NJ EMS Clinical Practice Protocols and Guidelines v1, effective 8/21/2025**, NJ DOH OEMS. https://www.nj.gov/health/ems/documents/NEWJERSEYEMSCLINICALPRACTICEPROTOCOLS_GUIDELINES_FINAL8.21.2025v1.pdf
- **N.J.S.A. 26:2H-129 et seq.**, Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment Act; **N.J.S.A. 26:2H-53 et seq.**, New Jersey Advance Directives for Health Care Act.
- **N.J.S.A. 30:4-27.1 et seq.**, involuntary commitment and screening services.
- NJ Out-of-Hospital DNR guidelines, NJ-ACEP and the Medical Society of New Jersey, **August 2003** (form and bracelet detail only; the 2025 protocol governs EMS action). https://www.njha.com/media/33214/DNRGuidelines.pdf

## When a patient exists

The protocols define **patient contact** as beginning when a crew member makes physical or verbal contact. They impose an affirmative duty to make every reasonable effort to access potential patients, and to fully document efforts to locate a patient when no patient is found.

## Adult refusal

A competent adult may refuse anything. New Jersey has no single statewide refusal form, so the content of your documentation is the protection.

**The one hard rule, from the behavioral emergencies protocol:** a patient who is a danger to self or others **may not refuse care**. If such a patient refuses and requires medical care, contact police and, if available, the local mental health crisis agency.

If the patient is not an immediate threat and refuses transport, the protocol directs you to encourage a mental health evaluation, avoid leaving them alone if possible, and assist in contacting responsible family or friends. The restraint procedure adds that you obtain a refusal of care for patients refusing transport.

### Capacity, in the order you assess it

1. **Correct the correctable.** Check glucose if your agency carries glucometers, give oxygen to the `94%` target, and reassess. Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury and hypoperfusion all impair capacity.
2. **Ask for understanding, not agreement.** Can they state the problem, the specific risk of refusing, and one alternative? Have them say it back.
3. **Look for coercion or intoxication.** Capacity is present-tense and task-specific.
4. **Document.** Alertness and orientation, vitals, glucose where indicated, the risks you explained in plain language including death, the number of times transport was offered, the offer to return, and the patient's own words.

> **Trap:** Patients given naloxone should be transported to the emergency department for further evaluation. Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does.

## Minors, from protocol 8.3

A **minor** is anyone who has not reached their eighteenth birthday. That legal definition is separate from the clinical terms pediatric patient, child and children.

- Treat under **implied consent** when the parent or authorized representative is unavailable. Except in life-threatening emergencies, attempt to reach the parent or guardian first.
- An authorized representative, for example a school or camp official expressly authorized by the parent, may consent.
- A parent or legal guardian may refuse care for a minor. When the guardian is not reasonably available, another adult family member or authorized representative having custody may refuse.
- A **telephonic refusal is acceptable** if you explain the consequences and document it carefully.
- A minor generally **may not** refuse. When one tries, enlist police, including a request for protective custody. Restrain only as a last resort.
- Contact medical command to discuss consent and refusal questions involving minors, and always attempt care in the minor's best interest.

### The three exceptions

1. A **minor parent** may consent to or refuse care for their own minor children if they have capacity to understand the treatment and consequences.
2. **Minors of any age** may give informed consent to treatment associated with rape, incest or sexual abuse.
3. An **emancipated minor** may consent or refuse, bearing the burden of establishing emancipation by documentation or otherwise.

## DNR and POLST, from protocol 8.4

The sequence, in order:

1. Conscious, alert patients: follow their wishes under standard consent procedures.
2. Patient unable to consent: determine whether a valid **Out-of-Hospital DNR** or **POLST** is present.
3. No form present: begin standard treatment.
4. Valid form present and applicable to the clinical state: follow the orders as written, including not beginning or terminating resuscitation.

Other advance directives, a living will, health care proxy, hospital DNR order or hospice status, are **not** field orders. Contact medical command early.

A copy of the original POLST or Out-of-Hospital DNR is valid.

| Feature | Out-of-Hospital DNR | POLST |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A physician order to withhold CPR | A portable medical order set covering treatment levels |
| When it applies | Pulseless, not breathing, unresponsive | Also applies when the patient has a pulse, is breathing, or is responsive |
| Validity | Completed and signed by the patient or surrogate and the attending physician or APN; approved bracelet accepted as evidence; copies acceptable | Physician or APN signature **and** patient or surrogate signature, license number on Section F; copies acceptable |
| Revocation | Destroying the form and bracelet, oral expression of intent by the patient, or by the attending physician or at the surrogate's direction | The patient or surrogate may void or modify the form |

### Reading a POLST

- **Section A** goals of care is **not** part of the order.
- **Section B** treatment level: Full Treatment, Limited Treatment, or comfort measures. Limited Treatment with "transfer to hospital only if comfort needs cannot be met in current location" means transport for comfort and symptom relief.
- **Section C** artificial nutrition.
- **Section D** the critical-patient section: attempt resuscitation or DNAR when pulseless or apneic; intubate or do-not-intubate for respiratory distress with a pulse. A do-not-intubate patient still receives other relief, oxygen, medications, and manual relief of airway obstruction.
- **Section E** names the surrogate decision maker.
- **Section F** signatures.

> **Key:** A blank box is not a refusal. The protocol states that if a box is left blank, the assumption is that treatment **will** be provided for that category.

EMS duties with a POLST: review it for completeness and validity, review the orders before starting treatment, clarify with the patient if they have capacity or with the surrogate, notify medical command, and bring the form with the patient, attaching a copy to your report.

## Involuntary commitment, the pathway behind the call

Under `N.J.S.A. 30:4-27.1 et seq.`, the Commissioner of Human Services designates **screening services** by county or region. A mental health screener with reasonable cause to believe a person needs involuntary commitment executes a **screening certificate**, which permits detention without a temporary court order for **no more than `72` hours**, during which the facility must initiate commitment proceedings. "Dangerous to others or property" means a substantial likelihood of serious bodily harm or serious property damage in the reasonably foreseeable future, judged on history, recent behavior, and any recent act, threat or serious psychiatric deterioration.

EMTs do not certify anyone. You recognize the pathway, use police when a patient cannot refuse because they are a danger, and hand off a behavioral description: what they said, what they did, what they have access to.

## Restraints, from protocol 6.5

Restraints must not cause undue physical discomfort, harm or pain. **Hard restraints such as handcuffs are prohibited unless the law enforcement officer who applied them personally accompanies the patient.** Patients are not restrained or transported in restraints unless the protocol's criteria are met or a physician or court authorized it. Document the reason, the type, the time applied, circulation checks, and any injuries. **At no time shall a patient be placed in the prone position.** Struggling against restraints can cause hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis and cardiac arrest.
